These pipelines were therefore applied to 18,787 individuals in the study sample. Data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study were considered high-quality based on their quality assessment protocols (Txt file= FreeSurfer QC; item= fsqc_qc; scan excluded if 0). This applied to 3,116 individuals in the study sample. For the remainder of the sample involving 15,504 participants, the T1-weighted images were downloaded and segmented locally, and the results were quality assessed using Qoala-T tool. As an additional assessment of image quality, we calculated the Euler number (EN), a reliable indicator that closely approximates the manual assessment of scan quality for the entire dataset.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: For diagnostic classification: Support vector classification (SVC) with linear kernel from scikit-learn (version 1.2.2); 5-fold cross-validation repeated 100 times; area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) averaged across folds; statistical significance established by comparing to null distribution from 1000 random permutations of diagnostic labels; pairwise ΔAUC calculated between models using Z-scores versus observed data and tested against null distribution using permutation. For symptom severity prediction: Ridge regression models with 100 repeats of 5-fold CV to predict PANSS scores; principal component analysis to reduce dimensionality to first 10 PCs explaining ≥90% variance; mean absolute error (MAE) averaged across folds as performance metric; pairwise ΔMAE calculated and tested against null distribution from permutations of PANSS scores.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: MFPR-derived normative models with non-linear age polynomials and linear global measures showed optimal performance and computational efficiency; Z-scores from these models significantly outperformed observed morphometric measures in diagnostic classification of early psychosis (AUC 0.63 vs 0.49, p<0.001) but showed no advantage for predicting symptom severity.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Across all 150 regional morphometric measures, MFPR, LMS, GPR, and WBLR showed comparable and statistically superior accuracy (MAE, RMSE, explained variance at PFDR<0.05) compared to GAMLSS, BLR, OLSR, and HBR, with MFPR having the shortest CPU time (<1 second vs 25-60 minutes for GPR). Optimal models used non-linear fractional polynomials of age and linear effects of global neuroimaging measures (ICV for subcortical volumes, mean cortical thickness for cortical thickness, total surface area for surface area). Scanner vendor, Euler number, and FreeSurfer version had minimal effects on performance. Model performance plateaued at sample sizes of approximately 3,000 participants. Age-bin sensitivity analyses showed correlation coefficients >0.98 between full-sample and age-bin-specific models across all ages (3-90 years). ComBat-GAM harmonization performed similarly to site-as-random-effect models. Longitudinal stability was excellent over ~2-year intervals (SLIM and QTAB cohorts). In clinical validation with HCP-EP, SVC using MFPR-derived Z-scores achieved AUC of 0.63 (p<0.001) for diagnostic classification, significantly outperforming SVC using observed data (AUC 0.49, chance level). However, ridge regression models for predicting PANSS psychotic symptom severity showed no above-chance performance for either Z-scores or observed data.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Limited representation of young and middle-aged adults; lack of long-term longitudinal follow-up data; generalizability to specific ancestries not tested; limited exploration of additional explanatory variables (e.g., childhood adversity, premature birth, socioeconomic status) that could improve model performance but may restrict applicability; cross-sectional compilation means samples at different ages had different exposures affecting brain health; later-life samples likely include survivors more resilient to mortality and morbidity
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: There are several methodological limitations pertinent to this study. Specifically, our study could benefit from the inclusion of more young and middle-aged adults and data from longitudinal follow-up over long periods of time. Testing the generalisability of our models to populations with specific ancestries is an important next step. We did not include an exhaustive list of potential explanatory variables. It could be argued that the inclusion of other variables, such as childhood adversity, premature birth, or socioeconomic status, which are known to influence brain morphometry, could have further improved model performance. ... On the other hand, the inclusion of multiple explanatory variables in the normative model itself could restrict its applicability to only those datasets in which all such features were assessed. ... In later life, samples of healthy individuals are likely to include those who are more resilient to mortality and morbidity.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study provides CentileBrain, a user-friendly web platform (https://centilebrain.org) that enables estimation of normative deviation scores from any sample with minimal technical and computing requirements using the optimized pretrained MFPR models. The platform provides model parameters as pretrained models in the context of open science. Sex-specific models were developed for all 150 regional morphometric measures. Sensitivity analyses included comparison of different GAMLSS models and software packages, supporting the superiority of the chosen implementation.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is a comprehensive algorithm benchmarking study rather than a typical clinical application study. The primary contribution is methodological: systematic comparison of 8 normative modeling algorithms (MFPR, OLSR, BLR, GAMLSS, LMS, GPR, WBLR, HBR) to identify optimal approaches. The sample is one of the largest normative modeling studies to date (N=37,407) spanning ages 3-90 years from 87 datasets across 20 countries. Quality control procedures varied by dataset source: ENIGMA protocols for 18,787 participants, ABCD protocols for 3,116 participants, and Qoala-T for 15,504 participants. The study establishes that sample sizes of ~3,000 are sufficient for robust normative models of brain morphometry. The MFPR algorithm emerged as optimal due to combined advantages in accuracy and computational efficiency. The study validated models both for longitudinal stability (SLIM and QTAB cohorts over ~2 years) and clinical utility (HCP-EP psychosis cohort). All models and code are made freely available through CentileBrain platform for open science. Supplementary materials include detailed dataset information (appendix 2), comprehensive algorithmic comparisons across all 150 regions, and multiple sensitivity analyses.
